title: Quantum–classical communication gaps for total functions
formal:
Do there exist real constants \(a\ge1\), \(\delta>0\), an integer \(b\ge1\), and an infinite set \(\mathcal N\subseteq\{2,3,\ldots\}\) such that, for every \(n\in\mathcal N\), some total Boolean function
\[f_n:\{0,1\}^n\times\{0,1\}^n\longrightarrow\{0,1\}\]
has bounded-error communication complexities satisfying
\[Q^*_{1/3}(f_n)\le a(\log_2 n)^b,
\qquad R_{1/3}(f_n)\ge a^{-1}n^\delta?\]
Here \(R_{1/3}\) permits classical public randomness and unrestricted interaction, and \(Q^*_{1/3}\) permits quantum communication and arbitrary finite prior entanglement. Only communication is charged. The constants are fixed independently of the input length and the function chosen at that length.

source_formulation.text: The imported passage is the background question on ITCS 2021 page 54:2 asking for exponential quantum advantage on total functions. This card makes its quantitative scale explicit as polylogarithmic quantum versus polynomial classical communication on an infinite family, matching the scale used in that source and in the new preprints. The source paper’s own main theorem additionally concerns efficient local players and partial functions; those extra restrictions are not part of the imported total-function question. Prior entanglement is permitted on the quantum side, and all classical interaction is allowed.

why: This asks whether the large quantum savings known for promise problems can persist for a Boolean function defined on every input pair. A positive family would refute any universal polynomial simulation of quantum communication by randomized classical communication, even when local computation is unrestricted.
status_note: Checked on 16 September 2026. Gavinsky arXiv:2608.18784v1 and Le Gall arXiv:2609.16726v1 claim total Boolean families with the displayed polylogarithmic quantum and polynomial randomized-classical costs. Their stated protocols/lower bounds match the free-entanglement, unrestricted-classical-interaction, per-input-error and worst-case-cost conventions here, allowing a final answer bit to Bob. The full PDFs and relevant scope were inspected, but the complete proofs have not been independently certified or Lean-checked. Status remains uncertain pending verification; the 2021 source-open statement is historical.

importance.reason: A central communication-complexity separation target isolating totality from promises and information cost from local computation; current matching preprint claims require an explicit status qualification.

sentences: Alice and Bob must compute a Boolean function defined on every pair of their binary inputs.
The target is an infinite family requiring polynomial randomized classical communication but only polylogarithmic quantum communication in the input length.
Local computation is free, classical public randomness and arbitrary interaction are allowed, and the quantum side may share input-independent entanglement.
The 2021 source’s separate efficient-player result concerns partial functions and does not impose an additional runtime condition here.
August and September 2026 preprints make matching total-function separation claims whose complete proofs remain unverified in this review.

definitions:
For a fixed function \(f:\{0,1\}^n\times\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\), Alice receives \(x\) and Bob receives \(y\). A protocol is fixed for the entire function before these inputs are chosen. Bob must output the bit \(f(x,y)\) with probability at least \(2/3\) for every pair \((x,y)\). Total means all \(2^{2n}\) pairs are included; no joint promise or relation with several acceptable outputs is allowed.

In a classical protocol the parties exchange bits and may use a shared random seed and private random bits, independent of the inputs. They have no shared entanglement. Each message and the final output depend only on the sender's own input, random information and received history. In a quantum protocol the parties exchange finite-dimensional registers consisting of qubits, may use arbitrary finite-dimensional local quantum operations and measurements, and may initially share any finite-dimensional entangled state independent of \((x,y)\). Local operations are completely positive trace-preserving maps, and the final output is a two-outcome measurement at Bob. Measurements may have classical outcomes stored locally. Transmitting a classical bit within a quantum protocol costs one qubit; communication is not hidden in a message's timing or length. Shared randomness and entanglement are not supplied as input-dependent advice, and postselection is not available.

Local computation, memory and preparation of input-independent shared resources are free. There is no bound on their complexity or on the finite dimension of prior entanglement. A protocol may depend nonuniformly on the full function \(f\). It uses a finite predetermined alternating schedule of transmissions, padding unused messages if needed, so a choice of schedule cannot convey information for free. Arbitrarily many rounds are permitted, subject to finite termination. The cost is the maximum total number of transmitted bits or qubits, over all input pairs and all random or measurement branches. \(R_{1/3}(f)\) and \(Q^*_{1/3}(f)\) are the least costs of protocols with the stated per-input error bound. These costs are finite because transmitting an entire input gives a finite deterministic protocol.

The family need exist only for infinitely many, hence arbitrarily large, input lengths. The constants \(a,b,\delta\) are common to all of them; the functions and their protocols may vary with \(n\). The display defines the precise polylogarithmic-versus-polynomial meaning of the exponential-advantage question used here. It does not require efficient local players, a uniform generator for the functions, one-way communication or a fixed number of messages. A stronger construction with any of these properties is allowed but not required.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the displayed family-existence proposition, or of its logical negation. A positive answer must specify admissible constants and an unambiguous infinite family, establish the quantum upper guarantee and prove the classical lower bound against every public-coin protocol in the stated model. A negative answer must establish that for every choice of the constants, only finitely many lengths admit a function satisfying both bounds. A separation only on promised input pairs, for relations, or against restricted-round classical protocols does not meet this target. A preprint theorem statement alone is not a checked proof.

context_blocks.text: Communication complexity studies two parties who can process their own inputs without charge but must pay for information exchanged. Thus an advantage measures transmitted information, not execution time. Total Boolean functions require one specified answer for every input pair; partial functions can exclude some pairs, and relations can permit several valid outputs. These distinctions are essential to interpreting a separation.

Girish, Raz and Tal’s ITCS 2021 work supplies a partial-function separation with efficient quantum players given oracle access to their inputs. Its introduction separately states that exponential advantage for total functions is open. The paper’s efficient-player theorem is a different statement from this card: importing its title as an extra runtime requirement would change the background question.

The chosen scale requires a classical cost growing as a positive power of \(n\), while quantum cost grows as a fixed power of \(\log n\). A fixed polynomial relation between the two communication costs is incompatible with such a family. The converse implication is not automatic: disproving every universal polynomial relation need not, by itself, yield this particular input-length scale.

Gavinsky's preliminary August 2026 preprint states an explicit total family with quantum cost \(O(\log^3 N\log\log N)\) and classical cost \(\Omega(N^{1/6}/\log^{7/3}N)\), where \(N\) is the per-party input length. These stated bounds fit the displayed scale after absorbing logarithmic factors into a fixed power and a slightly smaller positive exponent. The claimed quantum protocol has two messages and needs no prior entanglement; its classical lower bound permits unrestricted rounds.

Le Gall's September 2026 preprint claims a larger two-message separation, with \(\operatorname{polylog}(n)\) quantum cost and \(\widetilde\Omega(\sqrt n)\) randomized classical cost. It further states a classical lower bound \(\widetilde\Omega(n^{1-1/j})\) for every fixed integer \(j\ge2\), with a larger constant number of quantum messages. Its definitions explicitly allow public classical randomness and require worst-case communication and error at most \(1/3\) on each input.

A protocol without prior entanglement is admissible in the entanglement-assisted model, so that stronger resource restriction does not obstruct the claimed upper bound here. If the protocol outputs at Alice, sending the final answer bit to Bob adds only one unit of communication. These convention checks establish that the fresh claims match the target; they do not independently validate the new lower-bound proofs.

The matching claims are recorded with uncertain status. The original source, new full PDFs, theorem statements and relevant model conventions were inspected, but no complete independent proof certification or Lean verification was performed. The question has not been replaced by a stronger optimal exponent or an efficient-player variant merely because the new papers claim to answer it.
